==English==
{{wp}}

===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*gʷem-}}
{{etymon|en|:bor|frm:event<ety:inh<la:ēventus>>|id=occurrence|tree=1}}
From {{bor|en|frm|event}}, from {{der|en|la|ēventus||an event, occurrence}}, from {{m|la|ēveniō||to happen, to fall out, to come out}}, from {{m|la|ē||out of, from}}, short form of {{m|la|ex}} + {{m|la|veniō||come}}; related to {{m|en|venture}}, {{m|en|advent}}, {{m|en|convent}}, {{m|en|invent}}, {{m|en|convene}}, {{m|en|evene}}, etc.

====Pronunciation====
* {{IPA|en|/ɪˈvɛnt/|a=RP}}
* {{IPA|en|/ɪˈvɛnt/|/i-/|/ə-/|a=GA,CA}}
** {{audio|en|en-us-event.ogg|a=US}}
* {{IPA|en|/əˈvent/|a=AU,NZ}}
* {{IPA|en|a=North India|/ɪˈʋɛɳʈ/|/iːˈʋɛɳʈ/}}
* {{IPA|en|a=South India|/ˈiː.ʋɛɳʈ/}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɛnt|s=2}}

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{sid|en|occurrence}} An [[occurrence]]; something that happens.
#: {{syn|en|[[circumstance]] (''formal'')}}
#: {{ux|en|In the '''event''' of strong wind…}}
#* {{RQ:Macaulay Goldsmith|passage=the '''events''' of his early years}}
#* {{quote-book|en|title=Climate Change and the Health of Nations|author=Anthony J. McMichael; Alistair Woodward; Cameron Muir|year=2017|ISBN=9780190262952|page=67
|passage=Experience in Australia indicates that after a devastating weather '''event''', up to one-fifth of people suffer the debilitating effects of extreme stress, emotional injury, and despair.}}
# A [[prearranged]] [[social]] [[activity]] ([[function]], etc.)
#: {{ux|en|I went to an '''event''' in San Francisco last week.}}
#: {{ux|en|Where will the '''event''' be held?}}
# One of several contests that combine to make up a competition.
# An end [[result]]; an [[outcome]] (now chiefly in phrases).
#* {{RQ:Burton Melancholy|edition=2nd|partition=2|section=3|member=3
|passage=hard beginnings have many times prosperous '''events''' […].}}
#* {{RQ:Young Night-Thoughts|night=4
|passage=dark doubts between the promise and '''event'''}}
#: {{ux|en|In the '''event''', he turned out to have what I needed anyway.}}
# {{lb|en|figurative|uncommon|dated}} A [[remarkable]] [[person]].
#: {{syn|en|sensation}}
# {{lb|en|physics}} A point in [[spacetime]] having three [[spatial]] [[coordinate]]s and one [[temporal]] coordinate.
# {{lb|en|computing}} A possible action that the user can perform that is monitored by an [[application]] or the [[operating system]] (event [[listener]]). When an event occurs an [[event handler]] is called which performs a specific task.
# {{lb|en|probability theory}} A set of some of the possible outcomes; a subset of the [[sample space]].
#: If <math>X</math> is a random variable representing the toss of a six-sided die, then its sample space could be denoted as {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Examples of '''events''' could be: <math>X = 1</math>, <math>X = 2</math>, <math> X \ge 5, X \not = 4,</math> and <math>X \isin \{1,3,5\}</math>.
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} An affair in hand; business; enterprise.
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Measure|III|ii|passage=Leave we him to his '''events'''.}}
# {{lb|en|medicine}} An episode of severe health conditions.

===Etymology 2===
{{etymon|en|:der|fr:éventer|id=emit|text=+|tree=1}}

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|obsolete|intransitive}} To be [[emit]]ted or [[breathe]]d out; to [[evaporate]].
#* c. '''1597''', {{w|Ben Jonson}}, ''{{w|The Case is Altered}}'', Act V, Scene 8, in {{w|C. H. Herford}} and Percy Simpson (editors), ''Ben Jonson'', Volume 3, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1927, p. 178,<sup>[https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.182076]</sup>
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1615|author=[[w:William Barclay (writer)|William Barclay]]|title=Callirhoe; commonly called The Well of Spa or The Nymph of Aberdene|location=Aberdeen|year_published=1799|page=12|url=https://archive.org/details/b21695489
|passage=This is the reason why this water hath no such force when it is carried, as it hath at the spring it self: because the vertue of it consisteth in a spiritual and occulte qualitie, which '''eventeth''' and vanisheth by the carriage.}}

#* '''1559''', attributed to [[w:William Baldwin (author)|William Baldwin]], “How the Lorde Clyfford for his straunge and abhominable cruelty came to as straunge and sodayne a death” in ''{{w|The Mirror for Magistrates}}'', Part III, edited by {{w|Joseph Haslewood}}, London: Lackington, Allen & Co., 1815, Volume 2, p. 198,<sup>[http://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001017276]</sup>
